claims.text: Ti and V hydride precursors typically decompose at 400–600°C, depending on pressure.
Hydride decomposition should be followed by rapid heating to an extrusion temperature of 1000–1200°C.
Processing requires ultra-high vacuum below 10^-7 Pa or Ar/He with oxygen partial pressure below 10^-10 Pa.
Zr or Ti getters can capture residual oxygen originating from precursor decomposition or container outgassing.
Rapid post-decomposition cooling suppresses alpha-HCP formation and retains a metastable BCC solid solution.
Interstitial oxygen promotes nucleation of brittle alpha-HCP phases in Group IV-containing RHEAs.
Oxygen introduced during processing can produce TiO precipitates in NbMoTaWVTi.
The oxygen solubility limit is approximately 0.1 at% in Ti-based RHEAs.
Keeping oxygen partial pressure below the hydride equilibrium dissociation pressure and the matrix oxygen-solubility limit kinetically inhibits brittle-phase formation.
Rapid decomposition and extrusion produce and retain a BCC grain size below 1 µm.
Solid-solution strengthening and grain-boundary strengthening from a fine-grained BCC matrix increase the strength of NbMoTaWVTi.
Controlled aging at 800–1000°C for 1–2 hours can form coherent B2 or L21 precipitates without oxygen ingress.
The extrusion temperature must remain below 1300°C to avoid excessive grain growth and oxygen diffusion.
A strain rate of 10^-3 to 10^-2 s^-1 prevents adiabatic heating that could trigger localized oxygen diffusion.
The proposed process can produce bulk RHEA with greater than 99% relative density.
The proposed process can produce bulk RHEA without catastrophic cracking.
The resulting material will be single-phase BCC or BCC with controlled B2/L21 precipitates.
The processed alloy will have yield strength above 400 MPa at 1200°C.
The processed alloy will have room-temperature ductility above 5% because alpha-HCP formation is suppressed.
The hydride powder feed has an initial oxygen content below 50 ppm.
